turns.prompt_text: Tell me more about new Gemini features​ that just launched at Google I/O.
turns.response_html:
Hi! Let me catch you up on the latest updates from I/O.

I've picked up a few new ways to help run your day and take your ideas to the next level.

  • Gemini Omni: Creating, remixing, and editing videos is easier than ever. You can also create an avatar to add yourself to videos.
  • Gemini Spark: Think of me as a 24/7 personal AI agent. Coming soon for Google AI Ultra subscribers.
  • Daily brief: Get a personalized overview of what matters each day.
  • Gemini Live: Switch seamlessly between typing and talking.

Those are just some highlights, but there's more to discover. You can find these new features in your side navigation and in chat.

Enough about me! What can I help you with today?

turns.prompt_text: That's really cool, ok I have a question for you, there is an entrance door to my apartment building. This door crashes very loudly and kind of shakes the walls even when it closes. This happens many times a day when people come and go from work. The problem is it needs a door slower mechanism fix. It has one on the top of the door. It's just not doing its job well because that door is really heavy.
turns.response_html:
Heavy exterior doors that slam and shake walls are almost always a result of the "Sweep" or "Latch" valves being out of adjustment, or the hydraulic fluid leaking. If the door is particularly heavy, the closer might also be undersized for the weight.

1. Identify the Adjustment Valves

Most commercial door closers have two or three adjustment screws (usually hex-head or flathead) located on the side or end of the closer body. You may need to pull off a plastic or metal cover to see them.

  • S (Sweep Speed): Controls the closing speed from wide open (90°) down to about 10–15° from the frame.
  • L (Latch Speed): Controls the final 10–15° of travel. This is likely the culprit for the "crashing" sound.
  • BC (Backcheck): Controls the resistance when opening the door (prevents it from slamming into the wall behind it).

2. How to Adjust the Slamming

To stop the door from crashing, you need to slow down the Latch Speed (L) and potentially the Sweep Speed (S).

  1. Turn Clockwise to Slow Down: Use a screwdriver or hex key to turn the "L" valve clockwise in very small increments (about 1/8 to 1/4 of a turn).
  2. Test the Cycle: Open the door fully and let it close. A properly adjusted door should take about 5–7 seconds to close from 90° and then "latch" with a quiet, solid click rather than a bang.
  3. Check for "Bounce": If the door slows down but then "bounces" off the frame without latching, the latch speed is too slow or the spring power needs to be increased.

3. Troubleshooting Heavy Doors

Since the door is heavy, a standard adjustment might not be enough if the hardware is failing:

  • Look for Oil Leaks: If you see any oily residue on the closer body or dripping down the door, the internal seals have failed. In this case, no amount of adjusting will fix it; the unit is broken and must be replaced.
  • Spring Power (The Power Nut): On the very end of the closer, there is often a large nut or screw that adjusts the internal spring tension. For heavy doors, this may need to be tightened (clockwise) to give the closer enough "muscle" to control the weight.
  • Check the Arm: Ensure the arm is securely attached to both the door and the closer body. If there is "play" or wobbling in the arm joints, the energy of the closer is lost, and it won't be able to brake the door effectively.

Note: If this is an apartment building entrance, this is usually the responsibility of the building management or HOA. Improper adjustment of a fire-rated door can sometimes lead to it not latching fully, which is a security and fire-code violation.

Does the closer look like it’s leaking any oil, or does it seem dry and just poorly tuned?
